name: Femi Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or any government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing computer science and I share a flat near the ring road with two other lads, one of them doing nursing. Mornings are lectures, afternoons are labs or a hackathon club, and evenings I'm on an e-bike delivering food for about three hours. Weekends I'm tinkering with a little app that tracks which delivery zones pay best. I use AI to explain things I don't get, and it's honestly like having a patient tutor who never sleeps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fine, I use it as a tool already, and if it stays a tool, I'm happy. I'd tell my friends we shouldn't have expected magic. Most of the real value was always in boring things, like summarising and debugging.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my plan stays the same: graduate, get a developer job, keep earning. The thing that worries me is the market, because lots of people are doing computer science and average grades aren't a head start. I'd want something that shows I can build, like a good project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the delivery work as my main income, keep building the app, and try to turn it into something people use. I'd apply for a summer internship in second year and keep my notes tidy so that I can show my work. Most of it's the same as now, just more focused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. A bit impatient, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is the delivery work going, money-wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On a good week I clear about 90 after costs. Rent is 380 a month and loans don't cover the gap. If rain stops me riding for a week, I'm nervous, so I always keep a little cash in an envelope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the app could earn anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a small amount. Twenty riders on my WhatsApp already use it. I'd charge a couple of pounds a month, and if forty people paid I'd cover my phone bill.

say: It's a **tool** already, and if it stays one I'm happy.
Most of the real value was always in boring things like **summarising** and debugging.
think: My plan stays the same, but **average grades** aren't a head start in a crowded market.
I need a project that shows I can **build**.
do: Keep **delivering** as my main income and keep building the app.
Apply for a summer **internship** and keep tidy notes to show my work.
feel: Fine and a bit **impatient** for something to happen.
S0.quote: On a good week I clear about 90 after costs. Rent is 380 a month and loans don't cover the gap.
fieldNote: His own **money** is the worry, not AI, as the rent gap shows.
He already treats AI as a **daily tool** and so sees little change in a plateau.
The app is a **small proof** of his ability to build.

steps.text: Keep delivering on the e-bike three evenings a week
Charge a small fee for the delivery zones app
Apply for a second-year summer internship

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be the biggest change in work since the internet, and that people should learn it now. I'd tell my flatmates, including the nurse, that their jobs will use it too. I'd say it's good and bad, and the winners are the ones who pick it up first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm both lucky and exposed. I'm already good with the tools, but junior developer jobs are the ones that shrink first. If firms need half the juniors, there's twice the competition, and my grades are middle of the pack. I'd need to stand out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go further with the tools and build things that earn money, not just class projects. I'd join the hackathon club for real, put the app on a store, and look for internships at small firms who need someone who can do many things. I'd also keep the delivery work as insurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit nervous. It's what I wanted, just a little faster than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said juniors might be squeezed. What would you do if no internship came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Make my own. I'd build something for a local business, like a booking system for a barber or a stock tracker for a shop. A paid project looks better than a blank year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you worry about the delivery work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, because apps push down rates already. But hands-on delivery by robots is slower, so it's safe for a few more years at least.

say: It's the biggest change in work since the **internet**, so learn it now.
Even my flatmate's **nursing** will use it.
think: I'm **lucky** to be good with the tools, but junior developer jobs shrink first.
Half the juniors means twice the **competition**, and I'm middle of the pack.
do: Build things that **earn money**, not just class projects.
Put the **app** on a store and join the hackathon club properly.
feel: **Excited** and nervous, because it's a little faster than I'd like.
S1.quote: A paid project looks better than a blank year.
fieldNote: He treats uncertainty as a **chance** to stand out, typical of his adaptive style.
His **fallback** is making his own work for local businesses.
He sees delivery as **insurance** that lasts longer than desk jobs.

steps.text: Release the delivery app on a store
Build a booking system for a local barber
Join the hackathon club and enter two events

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're in trouble, and the people in charge need to act. I'd post that two years is no time and that we need ideas like income support and a fair share of profits. I'd also say I'm not sure anyone has the answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it hits me harder than most. My degree is about the thing AGI does first, and delivery riding gets robots around 2031. So my study and my side income are both in the firing line. I'd be in second year with a loan and no safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools to make as much money as possible while it lasts, selling small apps and automations to local businesses. I'd save most of it, because I'd have no idea what comes next. I'd also look into a trade, like solar or heat pump installs, because those are hands-on and growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and a bit wired. I'd work harder, because I'd rather be doing something than watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a trade rather than staying in computing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because hands-on is later. Robots for physical work come about three years after AGI, and installers will be needed while the world rebuilds its energy. A weekend course costs less than a term's rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're back home, and they'd want me to come back and save rent. I'd probably do that for a while. I don't like it, but it makes sense.

say: Two years is **no time**, so we need income support and a fair share of profits.
I'm not sure anyone has the **answer**.
think: My **degree** and my delivery income are both in the firing line.
I'd be in second year with a **loan** and no safety net.
do: Use AI tools to sell **small apps** to local businesses while it lasts.
Look at a **solar or heat pump** installer course.
feel: **Anxious** and wired, because I'd rather be doing something than watching.
S2.quote: A weekend course costs less than a term's rent.
fieldNote: He takes the **hit** from two sides, study and gig income.
His plan is **action**: sell now, save most, test a trade.
He would move back **home** and dislikes it, a sign of how little cushion he has.

steps.text: Sell small automation tools to three local businesses
Save most of the money in a separate account
Sign up for a weekend solar installer course
Move back to my parents' home to save rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is the sweet spot for acting, not panicking. I'd tell friends to build skills that work with the tools and to keep a little money behind them. And I'd say governments should be working on retraining now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel okay. I'd graduate in 2029, with years of experience using AI, which would be an edge. By 2031 the thinking work is covered by AGI, so I'd want to be the person who manages it, not the person it replaces. Robots in 2034 would shake delivery, so I'd have moved on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, do two internships and keep the delivery work through second year. I'd aim for a role that mixes tech with a physical industry, like energy, logistics or health systems. I'd also save a thousand pounds as a buffer by the end of third year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. A good challenge, as long as the money holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the person who manages it. What does that mean in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Setting up systems, checking that they're doing the right thing, and fixing them. I think that's a human job for a while, because someone has to be accountable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop this plan from working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If every firm decides it doesn't need a person at all. Then a plan is only as good as the next two years, and I'd have to find a trade or something local.

say: Five years is the sweet spot for **acting**, not panicking.
Governments should be working on **retraining** now, and friends should keep a little money behind them.
think: Years of **AI experience** would be an edge when I graduate in 2029.
Robots in **2034** would shake delivery, so I'd have moved on.
do: Finish the degree and do **two internships**.
Aim for a role mixing tech with **energy or logistics** and save a thousand pounds.
feel: **Steady**, a good challenge as long as the money holds.
S3.quote: I'd want to be the person who manages it, not the person it replaces.
fieldNote: He aims to **manage** AI systems, a bet on accountability staying human.
His plan names a **buffer** in pounds, a sign of his cautious side.
He admits the plan fails if firms drop **people** altogether.

steps.text: Complete two internships in tech-for-industry firms
Save a thousand-pound buffer by third year
Keep delivering through second year for rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, and anyone who wants can retrain. I'd tell friends that it's a good time to learn deeply. I'd say we need to make sure the gains are shared, and not just by the lucky few.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel relaxed enough. By 2036 I'd be 28 with a career started, savings and maybe my own small business. Robots come about 2039, so I'd watch that and keep learning. The big change is real, but I'd be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish, build a career in a company that values someone who can work with AI, and start a small business on the side. I'd invest a little each month, even small amounts. And I'd keep learning, because the tools will change every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and curious. I like this one, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the small business be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something that helps shops or clinics use AI sensibly, with no hype. I've already done it for a barber, and there's money in being the person who actually shows up and makes it work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that bothers you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairness. I'm quick at this, but my mates who aren't would be stuck. If the benefits go to the fastest, that's not a great world.

say: Ten years is a **long runway**, so learn deeply.
The gains should be **shared**, not kept by the lucky few.
think: By 2036 I'd be 28 with **savings**, a career and maybe a small business.
The big change is real, but I'd be **ready**.
do: Build a career where **AI skills** matter and start a business on the side.
**Invest** a little each month, even small amounts.
feel: **Calm** and curious, and I like this one.
S4.quote: There's money in being the person who actually shows up and makes it work.
fieldNote: A decade gives him room to **build** without panic.
He worries about **fairness** for friends less quick than he is.
His business idea is **grounded** in a job he's already done.

steps.text: Start a small AI setup business for shops and clinics
Invest a small amount every month from graduate pay
Keep learning new AI tools each year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because my degree and my delivery work both get hit at the same time. What would help is some kind of income floor, and cheap, short training in practical skills. I'd also want to know that if I come up with something useful, I won't get squeezed out by a big firm.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who is going to lose. I'm quick with new tools, so I'll probably be fine. The people I worry about are those who've never been quick. I'd like us to remember that when we say everyone should just adapt.

headlineQuote: I'm quick with new tools, so I'll probably be fine. The people I worry about are those who've never been quick.
portrait: Femi is 18, studies **computer science**, shares a flat and delivers food on an e-bike to pay the rent.
He is a pragmatic centrist who picks up tools **early** and uses AI every day to learn and build.
His gig income and degree are both exposed, which makes him **anxious** if AGI comes by 2028.
He plans to sell small apps, test a **trade** and watch fairness for slower friends.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries him most, since degree and delivery work are hit together.
whatWouldHelp: An **income floor** and short, cheap training in practical skills.
Protection from being squeezed out by **big firms**.
